Author: Y. Yu; F. Zhu; D. Wang; F. Tsung
Title: Empowering PHM Applications with Time Series Foundation Models: A Unified Multi-Task Learning Approach
Publication Title: 2025 IEEE 21st International Conference on Automation Science and Engineering (CASE)
Abstract Note: Currently, small, task-specific models dominate the development of Prognostics and Health Management (PHM) applications. However, these isolated models often struggle to address the diverse and fragmented requirements present in real industrial environments. The emergence of time-series foundation models has attracted considerable attention, providing a more flexible and effective approach for PHM applications. This study explores how time-series foundation models can enhance PHM applications. Using a typical aero-engine degradation dataset as the research context, we propose a novel unified multi-task learning approach that leverages pre-trained time-series foundation models. Specifically, we utilize these foundation models as the basis for time-series representation learning to tackle various PHM tasks. To accommodate the diverse requirements of these tasks, we design specialized output heads tailored for multi-task learning objectives. The pre-trained foundation model is then fine-tuned with specific datasets to develop localized task-specific models. We validate our approach through case studies using the C-MAPSS datasets. The experimental results demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of foundation models for the development of PHM applications.

Author: W. Zhan; L. Tao; Z. Zhao; Z. Huang; Z. Lian
Title: Exploration of Gearbox Multi-Step Remaining Useful Life Prediction based on LLM and PEFT
Publication Title: 2025 16th International Conference on Reliability, Maintainability and Safety (ICRMS)
Abstract Note: Gearboxes are essential components in mechanical systems, and accurately predicting their remaining useful life (RUL) is vital for implementing effective predictive maintenance strategies. In particular, multi-step RUL prediction facilitates the early detection of potential failures, thereby significantly improving system reliability and operational safety. However, existing lightweight deep learning models often face challenges in multi-step RUL prediction, primarily due to limited training data and constrained representational capacity. Recent advances in large language models (LLM) have shown remarkable generalization abilities and expressive embedding power, suggesting a promising new direction for addressing these limitations. In this study, we propose an end-to-end framework for multi-step RUL prediction of gearboxes, which harnesses the representational strengths of LLMs. The framework integrates parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) techniques to adapt LLMs effectively to time series forecasting tasks while maintaining computational efficiency. Experimental evaluations on a benchmark gearbox dataset demonstrate the superior performance and practical viability of the proposed approach.

Author: A. Carvalho; F. Boyle; J. Daly; J. Walsh
Title: Building Artificial Intelligence Agents with Large Language Models for Autonomous Interpretation of Equipment Sensor Data: P2
Publication Title: 2025 IEEE International Conference on Computation, Big-Data and Engineering (ICCBE)
Abstract Note: We presented a methodology for incorporating large language models (LLMs) into artificial intelligence (AI) agents capable of analyzing sensor and maintenance data to improve predictive maintenance tactics. We built on that foundation by moving from theoretical modeling to actual deployment, with a focus on real-time monitoring, adaptive learning, and agent scalability in live industrial applications. The new design prioritizes continuous data feeding, temporal analysis, and dynamic feedback loops, allowing the AI agent to adapt to changing equipment behavior and operational circumstances. The agent responds to emergent failure modes autonomously by combining LLMs with time-series anomaly detection, edge-to-cloud orchestration, and few-shot learning approaches, eliminating the need for substantial training. This stage also assesses deployment scenarios across many industrial systems, focusing on latency, reliability, and edge AI integration concerns. We investigated multi-agent collaboration and the implications of autonomous AI decisions in industrial contexts, emphasizing ethical and interpretability considerations under real-time limitations. This article focuses on real system integration, providing essential insights into the operationalization of LLM-powered agents for industrial AI.

Author: K. Abdelli
Title: Zero-shot forecasting of optical network telemetry using large language models
Publication Title: Journal of Optical Communications and Networking
Abstract Note: Accurate forecasting of optical network telemetry is critical for enabling predictive maintenance and proactive network management. However, conventional forecasting approaches often rely on task-specific architectures, extensive labeled datasets, and manual feature engineering—factors that limit their adaptability and scalability across heterogeneous deployment scenarios. In this work, we introduce a zero-shot forecasting framework that leverages pretrained large language models (LLMs) to perform prompt-based inference directly on telemetry data without requiring fine tuning, retraining, or supervision. Time series signals are tokenized at the digit level and reformulated as structured language sequences, enabling LLMs to perform forecasting, anomaly detection, and missing data imputation using natural language prompts. We evaluate our approach on real-world measurements from an aerial WDM system—comprising PM and SOP data under live traffic and varying environmental conditions—as well as on other out-of-distribution datasets. LLM demonstrates good forecasting accuracy and robustness to noise, missing inputs, and domain shifts, achieving performance that is competitive with classical and deep learning baselines across a range of metrics and conditions. Crucially, the model generalizes across multivariate and multimodal telemetry streams without architectural modification, enabling accurate forecasting from exogenous signals such as environmental variables. These results position instruction-tuned LLMs as lightweight, interpretable, and scalable building blocks for next-generation telemetry analytics—offering a unified, prompt-driven alternative to fragmented and model-centric forecasting pipelines.

Author: Dintén, R.; Zorrilla, M.
Title: Using Time Series Foundation Models for Few-Shot Remaining Useful Life Prediction of Aircraft Engines
Publication Title: CMES - Computer Modeling in Engineering and Sciences
Abstract Note: Predictive maintenance often involves imbalanced multivariate time series datasets with scarce failure events, posing challenges for model training due to the high dimensionality of the data and the need for domain-specific preprocessing, which frequently leads to the development of large and complex models. Inspired by the success of Large Language Models (LLMs), transformer-based foundation models have been developed for time series (TSFM). These models have been proven to reconstruct time series in a zero-shot manner, being able to capture different patterns that effectively characterize time series. This paper proposes the use of TSFM to generate embeddings of the input data space, making them more interpretable for machine learning models. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we trained three classical machine learning algorithms and one neural network using the embeddings generated by the TSFM called Moment for predicting the remaining useful life of aircraft engines. We test the models trained with both the full training dataset and only 10% of the training samples. Our results show that training simple models, such as support vector regressors or neural networks, with embeddings generated by Moment not only accelerates the training process but also enhances performance in few-shot learning scenarios, where data is scarce. This suggests a promising alternative to complex deep learning architectures, particularly in industrial contexts with limited labeled data. Copyright © 2025 The Authors.

Author: Chen, Y.; Liu, C.
Title: A sample-efficient transfer learning framework for industrial remaining useful life prediction leveraging large language models
Abstract Note: Remaining Useful Life (RUL) prediction is fundamental to industrial Prognostics and Health Management (PHM). However, existing models struggle to process high-dimensional, multi-condition sensor data, generalize across varying operating conditions, and perform well with limited labeled data. To address these challenges, we propose a sample-efficient RUL prediction framework based on a transferable Large Language Model (LLM), which captures complex temporal dependencies in sensor data while reducing pre-processing requirements. The framework integrates two core innovations: a transferable LLM backbone that automates feature extraction from complex sensor data, and a dual-score sample selection strategy that significantly improves learning efficiency by identifying the most informative samples for transfer learning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the framework achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance across diverse operating conditions using a single hyperparameter configuration, significantly reducing the computational overhead and domain expertise requirements that limit the scalability of existing methods. Beyond predictive accuracy, this study offers insights into its internal mechanisms, showing how it dynamically prioritizes sensor data to capture critical degradation patterns across varying conditions. These findings enhance model interpretability by linking data-driven predictions to physical processes. By addressing key challenges such as data efficiency, feature extraction, and transferability, the framework offers a reliable solution for industrial signal processing, improving the cost-effectiveness and robustness of PHM strategies across diverse operational domains. Author: Liu, X.; Lyu, Y.; Gao, J.; He, C.; Geng, M.; Fan, M.
Title: STL-LLM: A seasonal-trend decomposition-enhanced large language model for battery capacity aging trajectory prediction
Abstract Note: Reliable monitoring of lithium-ion battery health is critical for electric vehicles and energy storage systems. Accurate prediction of the remaining capacity aging trajectory remains essential for battery management, yet current machine learning approaches often fail to capture long-term temporal dependencies in degradation data or leverage heterogeneous datasets effectively. In particular, while Pre-trained Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit powerful reasoning abilities, their application to time-series-based capacity aging trajectory prediction is hindered by a fundamental modality mismatch. To address this, we propose STL-LLM, a novel framework integrating Seasonal-Trend decomposition using LOESS (STL) with frozen LLMs. STL-LLM disentangles battery health sequences into seasonal and trend components, reprograms these temporal features into text-aligned prompts, and employs prefix-based prompting to enhance temporal reasoning. The LLM's output is projected to generate a capacity aging trajectory prediction. Evaluations demonstrate STL-LLM's state-of-the-art accuracy across three public battery datasets, with consistent superiority in ablation and sensitivity studies. From a methodological perspective, STL-LLM offers a principled cross-modal representation learning solution for time-series forecasting, enabling frozen LLM deployment in non-text domains with minimal tuning. Practically, the framework provides a scalable and generalizable approach for battery prognostics, with potential applications in predictive maintenance and cloud-based battery management systems. More broadly, this work bridges the modality gap between structured time-series signals and pre-trained language models. It introduces a transferable paradigm for leveraging LLMs, which holds significant potential for advancing scientific time-series analysis and sequence modeling. While the direct application lies in battery health monitoring for new energy vehicles, this framework creates a pathway for broader impacts across energy systems. Copyright © 2026.
